overview: Ukraine declared independence in 1991 and confirmed it in a nationwide referendum. Its modern history includes scientific cooperation, creative communities and families building new lives after Soviet rule. Russia’s occupation of Crimea in 2014 and full-scale invasion in 2022 brought destruction and displacement, while Ukraine continued as an independent state.

sections.title: Science in space and in the classroom

items.text: Ukrainian payload specialist Leonid Kadenyuk flew aboard the space shuttle Columbia in November and December 1997. The mission carried ten plant experiments in the Collaborative Ukrainian Experiment. Studying living plants in microgravity connected Ukrainian researchers with an international crew and the practical challenges of growing things in space.

High-school students in Ukraine and the United States joined the 1997 project from their classrooms. They built versions of the flight equipment and studied Brassica rapa plants while Kadenyuk performed the experiment in orbit. Their plants became Earth-based comparisons for plants having a much more unusual school trip.

One pollination tool used a dead bee attached to a toothpick. The technique had been tried on the Mir space station and was repeated during STS-87 and in participating schools. Carefully moving pollen between flowers was part of the experiment: space gardening still needed someone to do the bee’s job.

Petrykivka painters decorate homes, household objects and musical instruments with flowers and other natural forms transformed by imagination. Birds can symbolize light, harmony and happiness. A cupboard or instrument can therefore carry a whole painted garden, including flowers that no botanist will find growing outside.

The 2013 UNESCO account describes Petrykivka painting being taught in local schools from preschool to college, as well as passed between generations. Children learn patterns and their meanings while developing their own skill. Family art can become classroom work, with older practitioners sharing techniques with interested newcomers.

To make a pysanka, an artist draws patterns in wax on an egg and dips it in dye. The wax keeps those areas from taking the new colour. Repeating the process builds a design in stages: the final egg contains a small history of places where colour was allowed, or politely refused, to go.

Decorated eggs can carry personal wishes and become gifts for a birth, christening or wedding. Families pass on patterns and take pride in their work; classes and workshops teach the skills too. UNESCO’s 2024 inscription includes both Ukraine and Ukrainian communities in Estonia, showing how a tradition travels with people.

Ukrainian borscht has many versions, made with broth and ingredients such as beetroot or fermented beet juice. Children can help relatives prepare it, and it is often served with bread or garlic buns. UNESCO placed the cooking tradition on its urgent-safeguarding list in 2022 because war and displacement threatened the communities and ingredients that sustain it.

In a February 2025 UNICEF account, younger pupils in Pavlohrad were learning together in a basement converted into classrooms. Warmth, light and running water helped make lessons possible while the city faced attacks. Older children still had to study remotely. Returning to school meant seeing friends as well as opening exercise books.

Keeping taps running requires electricity as well as pipes. A September 2026 UNICEF report describes upgraded Kyiv pumps that adjust to water pressure and generators that start during power cuts. Laboratory staff also check water quality. Their work supports drinking, washing, school kitchens, toilets and hospitals: an ordinary tap depends on many skilled people.

The independence referendum of 1 December 1991 involved nearly 31.9 million voters. About 90.32 percent of those participating supported independence, with turnout around 84.18 percent. These are different measurements: one tells us how participants voted, while the other tells us how many eligible voters came to the polls.

Ukrainian Cyrillic in the independence act of 24 August 1991: “Територія України є неподільною і недоторканною.” Translation: “The territory of Ukraine is indivisible and inviolable.” The wording is preserved in Parliament’s official electronic text of the act, a short statement about the new state’s territory.

ending.text: Ukraine continues as an independent state. Russia’s invasions and occupation have not lawfully extinguished its sovereignty. The map’s outline represents internationally recognized territory, including Crimea, rather than a real-time line of military control. The 1994 label begins this imported map record; independence dates to 1991.
